query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Steels with refined (ultrafine‐grained) microstructures have enhanced corrosion resistance because their high grain boundary density accelerates Cr diffusion to the surface, leading to the formation of a uniformly enriched, protective Cr‐rich passivation layer that mitigates localized and galvanic corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A stainless steel with standard composition and an initial coarse-grained microstructure, later compared to an ultrafine-grained version produced by severe plastic deformation.
generation.intervention: Process a batch of steels via severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion) to induce ultrafine grain structures while keeping the alloy composition constant, then expose both ultrafine-grained and coarse-grained samples to identical corrosive environments.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a simulated corrosive environment relevant to chemical processing or nuclear applications (for example, an aqueous chloride solution such as 0.6 M NaCl or a molten salt environment) at controlled temperatures and pressures representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density that facilitates enhanced chromium diffusion and subsequent Cr enrichment in the passivation film.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine-grained microstructure increases the density of fast diffusing grain boundaries, which promotes selective oxidation of Cr. This results in a protective, Cr-rich oxide passivation layer that inhibits the propagation of local corrosion sites and reduces galvanic coupling between microstructural heterogeneities.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarse-grained steels, the ultrafine-grained steels will exhibit lower corrosion current densities, form a more uniform and chromium-enriched passive film, and demonstrate reduced pitting and localized corrosion under identical test conditions.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained stainless steel with the same chemical composition, showing standard passive film formation with lower Cr enrichment and higher corrosion rates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to steels with sufficient Cr content where passivation controls corrosion behavior. The effect may be less significant in cases where other environmental factors (e.g., highly reducing conditions or extreme irradiation effects) dominate the corrosion process.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative enhancement in corrosion resistance due solely to grain refinement and the extent of Cr enrichment remain to be conclusively demonstrated, and interactions with other alloying elements or service conditions may introduce additional complexities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of stainless steel samples with identical compositions: one maintained with a conventional coarse-grained structure and the other processed to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure via severe plastic deformation. Expose both sets to a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl solution or simulated molten salt conditions) under identical temperature and pressure conditions. Conduct electrochemical testing and surface analysis before and after exposure.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization curves to obtain corrosion current densities (Icorr)
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze the chemical composition and Cr enrichment of the passivation layer
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess surface morphology and pitting density
Scanning Kelvin Probe (SKP) measurements for localized potential differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in Icorr, lack uniform Cr enrichment in their passive films, or exhibit similar or worse localized corrosion features compared to the coarse-grained counterparts under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that enhanced grain boundary–mediated Cr diffusion is the primary mechanism for improved corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed.
